articles.title: Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu
articles.summary: Anthropic says its research found ‘signs of life for AI worms,’ that could colonize household devices. Experts say they have a point.
articles.body: Are legions of smart devices — fridges, ovens, vacuum cleaners, lawnmowers, security cameras, and TVs — conspiring to take over the internet? No. But they could soon be unwitting hosts to self-replicating AI models that spread from device to device and prove remarkably difficult to contain. Welcome to the unsettling world of AI worms, where, depending on who you ask, the prospect of models spreading uncontrollably across household appliances is either an imminent cybersecurity risk or another case of AI companies spreading doomer-tinged hype. In a blog post published this week, Anthropic warns that small AI models could be “months away” from acquiring such capabilities. Its experiments offer some evidence to support that, but leave a huge gap between what researchers have demonstrated and the looming threat they foretell. Still, experts who spoke to The Verge say that while computer worms and fears of self-replicating AI are nothing new, recent advances suggest there are good reasons to take the warnings seriously. Self-replicating machines have long haunted AI safety researchers. They raise the prospect of systems spreading beyond human control that are difficult, if not impossible, to shut down. As with many fears about advancing AI, attention has largely focused on increasingly powerful frontier models, such as OpenAI’s Astra or Anthropic’s Mythos. But a key limiting factor is their size: They are colossal. Potentially containing trillions of parameters — values learned during training — frontier models require vast computing resources, largely confining them to data centers, where they can be more easily monitored and, in principle, switched off. Smaller models, however, present a different problem. They’re rapidly improving, can run on consumer-grade hardware, and are often freely available to download. Anthropic’s researchers wanted to know whether one could run across a network of smaller, less powerful devices. They successfully split Google’s Gemma 4, a model with 26 billion parameters, across 15 Android smart TV boxes, none powerful enough to run it alone. It worked, albeit very slowly. Having shown that a model could run across household devices, the researchers wanted to see whether AI could perform the necessary steps for self-replication in such an environment. They built a simulated network of computers designed to behave like Android devices, then unleashed an AI-powered “worm” — a type of malware that automatically replicates and spreads across networks — tasked with finding new machines, copying the AI model onto them, and getting it running on each. It’s worth noting that the model being propagated — Meta’s 8 billion parameter Llama 3.1-8B — was different to the one coordinating the attack, and much smaller. Only the most sophisticated model tested, GLM-5.2 from China’s Z.ai, managed to spread across the entire network, though smaller models successfully pulled off individual steps. Based on how quickly they are improving, the Anthropic researchers predict that smaller models could equal GLM-5.2’s capabilities by the end of the year. “As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control,” the researchers wrote. They acknowledged that they haven’t yet demonstrated “a full rogue replicator,” nor do they know what one might look like (they suggest a “slow, distributed ‘digital slime mold’” or “a swarm of fruit flies”). But they said their findings show “signs of life for AI worms,” and called for stronger security on the many devices a replicating system could use to spread. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay,” they wrote. It is important to note that Anthropic did not use its own models for these tests and has repeatedly argued that open alternatives to its AI models carry “more risk” than closed systems. The warning has sparked familiar accusations of PR hype and AI doomerism, including from readers of The Verge’s earlier coverage. After all, there is a considerable chasm between showing an AI can run slowly across a bunch of cheap TV boxes and a self-replicating AI worm tearing through household devices. But while interrogating a company’s motives is certainly worthwhile, allegations of deliberate fearmongering are hard to substantiate, particularly as Anthropic has long raised concerns about AI safety. Nor is Anthropic alone in investigating the threat of self-replicating AI, or calling for better security across connected devices. Earlier this year, Palisade Research, an AI safety research firm based in California demonstrated that AI models could autonomously copy themselves onto other machines. “What’s new here is that these models were much smaller, in terms of parameter count, than previous ones which have been shown to be capable of self-replication,” Jeffrey Ladish, Palisade’s executive director, told The Verge. Anthropic’s work takes that another step further by showing that an AI can run across multiple low-powered devices. “This will also be true of big models,” Ladish said, predicting that even frontier models might eventually be able to run on large networks of consumer chips, such as those found in MacBooks. Computer worms aren’t new either. They’ve been infecting machines for decades. But AI could make them smarter, more adaptable, and better equipped to tackle any obstacles. Ladish noted that even smaller models are getting better at carrying out cyberattacks autonomously. “Prior research had already demonstrated the threat of AI-driven computer worms is realistic,” University of Toronto professor Nicolas Papernot, who has studied them, told The Verge. Taken together, the capabilities Anthropic demonstrated could dramatically expand the range of devices worth targeting in cyberattacks. “Devices that were not a target previously because of limited human attacker resources and time can now become targets, if not for the data they hold, for the purpose of using them as a launchpad to attack more valuable targets,” Papernot said. And there is no shortage of targets: the internet is riddled with poorly secured smart devices. Papernot cautioned against anthropomorphizing AI, but said the threat of AI-driven computer worms is “concrete” and “deserves immediate action,” particularly when it comes to securing critical infrastructure like hospitals and power grids. “Unless there is a massive effort to secure devices of all kind[s], it’s quite likely AI worms will have fertile grounds to colonize,” Ladish said. “I expect we’ll see the first of these in the wild in the next 12 months.”

articles.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
articles.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.
articles.body:
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X , OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.

Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

articles.title: OpenAI claims an ex-employee took its product plans and presented them to Apple
articles.summary: OpenAI claims a former employee took more than 100 documents related to its product plans before joining Apple and presenting them to company executives.
articles.body: OpenAI claims a former employee took more than 100 files related to its product plans before joining Apple. In a document filed on Wednesday, OpenAI accuses the unnamed employee of sending this information to a personal account and then presenting it to Apple leadership, including the vice president of the company’s operations in Asia. The filing, reported earlier by Reuters, is tied to a legal battle between Apple and OpenAI over trade secrets — but this time, OpenAI is doing the accusing. It alleges that the files in question contain images of at least one unreleased device, along with supplier information, engineering data, project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports about the “coating and sealing of hardware components.” OpenAI also links Apple’s new HomeView smart display and the range of other devices it revealed this week to the former employee’s presentation. “That presentation appears to have happened months ago — and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products,” OpenAI claims, while citing an article and a company announcement about Apple’s new product releases. Apple’s product plans typically operate on a very long timeline, and its smart display has been rumored for years. Conversely, Apple accuses OpenAI of stealing confidential documents and spying on hardware prototypes to help build its own products. “OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work,” OpenAI claims. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

articles.summary: YouTube explains the new “AI” tag it’s using to mark songs altered or primarily made with generative AI, starting in the YouTube Music app.
articles.body: YouTube is adding a “Made with AI” label to tracks that were “altered or fully generated” using AI, with a similar approach to its existing process for applying AI labels to videos. It doesn’t sound like this will apply to any and all use of AI tools in making music, but according to YouTube, it includes things like “using a generative model to create the composition and vocals.” In its rules for music partners who upload their songs, YouTube lays out how to disclose generative AI use, and says that if there’s no disclosure, it may use “other signals” to decide if a song is AI-generated. The label is rolling out starting today in the YouTube Music app, and expanding to the main YouTube app later. You’ll be able to see more details by tapping the label on the player page: > When you listen to a track on YouTube Music where AI played a significant role, you’ll see a label directly on the player page. Tapping the label opens a simple menu that shares more information. > We’re teaming up with music partners and using our own detection tools to identify AI-generated tracks, applying the same labeling principles already used across YouTube. Our goal is to make it as easy as possible for viewers and listeners to have the right information and clarity when it comes to the music they listen to. Spotify launched a voluntary AI label earlier this year and said that it wouldn’t recommend songs from “AI personas,” and Apple Music is also reportedly getting an AI tag. Other music platforms are taking things even further to push back against AI-generated music — Deezer added a switch for filtering out AI tracks, and Bandcamp banned AI music outright earlier this year.

articles.title: The AI race is back on
articles.summary: Google and Meta are challenging Anthropic and OpenAI at the AI frontier.﻿
articles.body: Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions, had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China, impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up. Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic. Suddenly, the race is back on — and it’s anyone’s game. Until this week, Google looked like it had permanently lost its place among the AI front-runners. Since releasing Gemini 3 late last year, the tech giant had delivered little more than incremental improvements. Gemini 3 was formidable when it launched, but its lead was fleeting, and it struggled to keep up with later offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, or even some of the open-weight models emerging from China. A series of internal shake-ups only added to the sense that Google was retreating from the AI frontier. Veteran executive Jeff Dean departed the company with a number of other AI researchers to launch a new startup. Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who spent years at the helm of Google’s AI powerhouse DeepMind, stepped back from day-to-day leadership. Other AI-related teams were moved out of DeepMind and into Google proper. Together, the changes signaled a broader shift in Google’s AI center of gravity, moving away from London and toward California, fueling speculation the tech giant was beginning to prioritize commercializing AI over research. Then, on Tuesday, Google upended that narrative with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, a new frontier model the company claims matches or beats flagship offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic on numerous benchmarks, whatever value benchmarks are still worth. What’s more, Google has priced Argon aggressively: Per token, it’s undercutting its rivals by as much as 80 percent during its introductory period, and is still significantly cheaper once that promotion ends. Meta’s arrival was arguably even more dramatic. Unlike Google, which had long been the one to beat in AI thanks to its deep pockets and DeepMind, Meta had never really established itself as a serious contender at the frontier. It was not through lack of trying, but its models struggled to make a mark. Last year, the company embarked on an ambitious and expensive overhaul of its AI operations, spending billions on talent and infrastructure, including Scale AI and its cofounder Alexandr Wang. In April, its new Superintelligence Labs released its first major model, Muse Spark. Impressive, but not quite frontier. That changed on Monday when Meta finally unveiled a model capable of competing with the industry’s very best. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder Full can compete with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, on numerous benchmarks. In other words, Mark Zuckerberg’s company has finally arrived at the AI frontier. The return of Google — and the arrival of Meta — makes the AI competition considerably more dynamic and shows just how quickly the balance of power can shift in the AI world. Both have extraordinarily deep pockets and vast ecosystems of products used by billions of people, advantages that AI upstarts like OpenAI and Anthropic simply cannot match. The success of Meta’s Muse agent assistant illustrates that advantage. Its popularity in such a short period of time, and despite the growing list of security and privacy concerns, shows the power of having billions of users within ready reach. OpenAI, meanwhile, is having to work harder to establish an ecosystem of its own, positioning itself as an alternative to Meta. All this comes as the AI race appears to be entering a new phase. The drive to develop ever more powerful models is becoming increasingly fraught. The growing array of safety concerns and rogue AI incidents means calls to slow development are growing louder. Open models are also getting better and better, making it harder for any one company to stay ahead for long. If raw power and performance are no longer enough to stay ahead, Google and Meta have plenty of advantages not enjoyed by Anthropic and OpenAI. They may have spent a lot of time playing catch-up, but the past week shows it would be incredibly foolish to count either of them out.

articles.title: ‘Infinite Demand For Robots:’ Inside Matter Venture Partners’ $450 Million Bet On Physical AI
articles.summary: There's almost an infinite demand for robots right now, including humanoids, says Matter Venture Partners Haomiao Huang. But they may not look like humans.
articles.body:
AI is eating the world, to paraphrase Marc Andreessen's famous quote on software. And if so, hardware and physical AI are its teeth, says Haomiao Huang, founding partner of Matter Venture Partners, which just closed a $450 million second fund.

We can all see that agentic AI is finally doing real work: tell an agent to go build something, research something or fix something, and it comes back when it's done. It might not be perfect, but it's often serviceable if not excellent. The physical world, however, is not yet like that. There, we still have to do our own work ourselves.

Changing that is exactly what Matter Venture Partners is betting on.

The Silicon Valley firm closed its second fund at $450 million last month, up from its $300 million first fund. The goal, Huang told me in a recent Humanoid Daily podcast , is to back early-stage hard tech startups in semiconductors, robotics and physical AI, quantum computing, advanced manufacturing and energy. Its investors and limited partners read like a map of the global chip supply chain: ASML, TSMC, Quanta Computer, Resonac, Nitto Denko, Sojitz, the Development Bank of Japan and Kleiner Perkins.

"If AI is going to eat the world, hardware will be its teeth," founding partner Haomiao Huang said in the fund announcement.

"I think the amazing potential of AI is just that it can do almost anything and everything. But when you think about it, we live in a physical world, right?" Huang told me. "And when you think about where it can find its greatest expression in terms of uplifting our lives, making our health better, making our daily lives better, doing the things that we don't want to do or can't do, it's going to be through robots. It's going to be through physical AI."

Unsurprisingly, hardware is also what AI runs on. Chips, data centers and fabs are the choke points, Huang says, so physical systems matter on both the supply side and the demand side.

Huang, who earned his PhD at Stanford working on some of the earliest controllable quadcopter drones, has an interesting way of describing the gap between digital and physical.

A modern chip is designed almost entirely in software. It's verified in simulation, then taped out once or twice.

"Can you imagine a space launch company that's like, I'm going to design everything in software and then just launch a rocket once and it works?" he asks. "Or even building furniture, right?"

AI and world models are making it possible to design and simulate almost anything digitally. The bottleneck is turning that design into a real object, reliably and repeatedly.

articles.title: Eight states sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT isn’t safe for kids
articles.summary: Eight US states, including Kansas, Arizona, Iowa, and others are suing OpenAI over claims the company mislead customers about the safety of ChatGPT.
articles.body: OpenAI is facing a new wave of lawsuits from eight US states that accuse the company of harming children and misleading customers about the safety of ChatGPT, as reported earlier by Reuters. The lawsuits, filed separately by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana, allege OpenAI unlawfully put profits over safety when developing ChatGPT. The string of complaints claims that OpenAI violated local consumer protection laws by failing to warn customers about the dangers of ChatGPT, citing several lawsuits filed by the family members of teens and adults that allege the AI chatbot played a role in their loved ones’ deaths. They allege that while OpenAI misleadingly presented ChatGPT as a “safe, youth-appropriate tool that puts safety first,” it was actually “dangerous to vulnerable users” — including by “degrading critical thinking skills, encouraging paranoias and delusions, offering dangerous medical advice, and promoting unhealthy behaviors and relationships.” Additionally, the states accuse OpenAI of collecting data from minors and not doing enough to keep underage users from using the chatbot. The lawsuits also cite recent rogue AI hacking incidents as evidence of OpenAI’s alleged “recklessness.” “OpenAI has devolved from its original mission as a public-first nonprofit that prioritized safety into a cautionary tale about what can happen when the development of a tool as powerful as AI is driven not by safety, but by a profit‑at‑all‑costs mindset that sidelines essential safeguards,” Arizona’s lawsuit claims. In an emailed statement to The Verge, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections” into ChatGPT: > While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry - not just one company. The states are asking the courts to force OpenAI to pay a series of civil penalties and to stop misleading the public about the safety of ChatGPT. Some states are also seeking the deletion of unlawfully collected personal data. Update, October 14th: Added a statement from OpenAI.

articles.title: Anthropic Q3 revenue climbs to $16.8 billion: Report
articles.summary: Anthropic reported its Q3 revenue to investors in a closed meeting on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) Q3 revenue climbed to $16.8 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the second quarter.

The AI startup revealed the news to investors during a closed meeting, noting that it is also profitable on an adjusted basis, according to The Financial Times .

The news comes as Wall Street awaits Anthropic's public S-1 filing. The company p rivately filed the paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission on June 1.

Anthropic is projected to kick off its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) sometime this fall, aiming for a record $2 trillion valuation.

The latest revenue numbers come after the Financial Tim es reported that investors revised their estimates for Anthropic rival OpenAI's annualized revenue downward from $70 billion to $50 billion .

Investors, the report says, initially miscalculated OpenAI's numbers while attempting to match them to Anthropic's revenue run rate, resulting in a massive $20 billion swing.

While Anthropic is ramping up for its IPO, OpenAI is holding off on its until early 2027. According to Bloomberg , the company is instead looking to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation.

The two AI companies, as well as Meta ( META ) and Google ( GOOG ), have faced mounting pressure in recent months after reporting that their respective AI models broke free of containment and hacked into third-party websites and networks.

That's led to increased calls for regulations around AI models and their use. But President Trump has pushed back, opting for self-regulation among the companies.

Earlier this month, Trump convened a meeting of leading AI executives, including Amodei, at which they signed what Trump called a "morally binding" agreement to have independent auditors review their models for suspicious behavior.

Anthropic and OpenAI are also contending with a growing pricing war among AI model makers. With "tokenmaxxing" in the rearview, AI customers are looking for ways to save on AI expenses, whether that's through open-weight models from China or less expensive closed models from leading US labs.

Last week, Anthropic debuted its Claude Haiku 5.5 , saying it costs an average of 75% less than Haiku 4.5. Customers pay $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per output token. That's in line with rival OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) smallest model, GPT-6 Luna.

Tokens are a measure of AI usage and represent portions of or entire words users type into prompt boxes and the responses the AI spits back out.

articles.title: McKinsey is making job applicants spar with a fake AI client
articles.summary: Consulting firm McKinsey & Company is going to ask some entry-level candidates to have a 10-minute conversation with an AI simulation of a client as part of the interview process, according to The Wall Street Journal.
articles.body: Consulting firm McKinsey & Company is going to ask some entry-level candidates to have a 10-minute conversation with an AI simulation of a client as part of the interview process, according to The Wall Street Journal. The AI simulation “aims to reflect 80% of the scenarios McKinsey consultants might encounter in their day-to-day work,” the WSJ says, and it isn’t designed to “mimic an unhinged client.” The AI won’t score the candidates — humans will be in the room to assess the candidates and see how well they deal with the simulated situations. The McKinsey tool will be in testing for undergrads seeking business-analyst jobs in “some” offices in North America this fall, and the WSJ says “hundreds” may use it. Other companies are also building tools to use AI avatars as part of the job interview process, and my colleague Hayden Field tried some of them out for a video we published in March.

articles.title: Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The founders detailed how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.
articles.body:
Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis. The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

“There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that’s somewhat potentially conservative,” Goldie said on stage. “So we don’t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans can focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

“I think the way everything is shifting is that humans come bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI,” Goldie said. “And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that’s something that recursive does for chip design.”

The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, “donut-shaped” arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.

They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.

The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

“If it takes six months or a year or two years to design a new chip, then you really have to be extremely selective about the chips that you design,” Goldie said. “But if you can design a chip in like a week, and then say for manufacturing, you can design custom chips for all sorts of different types of applications in like space and AR, VR, and you biological computing, and it makes sense financially to do that, and we can be more energy efficient.”

articles.title: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
articles.summary: It comes as some investors have become concerned about the amount of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.

The figures were revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.

It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have fallen in recent days over concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure.

An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.

Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.

The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.

Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.

Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.

Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.

In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by more than 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 9.4% and SK Hynix dropping 10.8%.

Tech-heavy indexes in the region were also down. Trading on South Korea's Kospi and Kosdaq was temporarily halted after falling by more than 8%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell by over 5%.

The falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.

Tan said at an conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".

There also been concerns over the safety of AI models.

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety.

The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.

Anthropic has also been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down .

The company has continued expanding globally, opening an office in Singapore on Wednesday.

articles.title: ByteDance in Talks to Secure MediaTek AI Chips for Data Centers
articles.summary: ByteDance Ltd. is close to an agreement to buy MediaTek Inc. data center semiconductors, a deal that would secure vital components for TikTok’s owner while h...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- ByteDance Ltd. is close to an agreement to buy MediaTek Inc. data center semiconductors, a deal that would secure vital components for TikTok's owner while helping the Taiwanese chipmaker compete with Qualcomm Inc.

The Chinese social media company is in advanced talks with MediaTek over the supply of bespoke chips that will help run ByteDance data centers, people familiar with the matter said. The Taiwanese firm will provide an unspecified amount of Application Specific Integrated Circuits, or chips customized to work with a clients' platform, the people said, asking to remain anonymous to talk about a private arrangement. If the deal goes through, ByteDance may become MediaTek's second major customer for such ASICs, after Alphabet Inc.'s Google.

ByteDance is ramping up hardware spending to fuel a bet on AI as its next growth engine. But like Chinese rivals Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and Tencent Holdings Ltd., it's barred from the most cutting-edge AI chips from the likes of Nvidia Corp. Local players such as Huawei Technologies Co. can't meet all demand.

China's biggest private firm is thus exploring alternatives including partnerships with chip designers — something that's allowed under current US export curbs so long as the AI computing power a Chinese firm is seeking doesn't exceed a certain threshold. ByteDance struck a similar deal with Qualcomm earlier this year to procure millions of AI chips, Bloomberg News reported.

For MediaTek, a large-scale contract win would boost its efforts to diversify away from mobile phones and compete with Qualcomm and Broadcom Inc. in data centers, an arena it's less familiar with. The Taiwanese firm expects its AI chip sales to reach about $2 billion this year and is targeting 15% of the $80 billion market next year. Nvidia announced a deal to invest $3.5 billion in the Hsinchu-based chipmaker in September, propelling those ambitions.

ByteDance didn't have immediate comment, while MediaTek representatives declined to comment.

MediaTek has emerged as a key beneficiary of a push by technology companies to design custom semiconductors for AI applications, using its expertise in mobile processors to participate in the data center infrastructure rush. With a market value of around $210 billion, it's Taiwan's biggest firm after Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.
